title: Monster Arena - SDF blend shells
author: Karmaroo2020
selftext:
Monster Arena is a browser game — no install, no launcher, you roll a monster and fight for ladder position. [monsterarena.gg](https://monsterarena.gg) \- The premise is that you can take position on the ladder and set up a defense so even when you are gone your monster can accept challenges (and terms) and fight while you are away.    
  
The monsters aren't sprites or premade models. They're SDF blend shells, a few dozen primitives per body, so parts actually fuse instead of being stuck together. The generator picks body plan, proportions, colors, coat, etc.  I did use Blender's MCP to build out the arena biomes 3D structure but no texture assets exist in game. 

Trailer's all in-engine. I had to build a capture rig for it because normal screen recording was useless: the render loop stops running itself and a script steps one frame at a time, so it doesn't matter how slow the machine is.

I directed, agents wrote the code.  I started with a scalable client/server architecture and data model.  Built for multiplayer.  Supports mobile as well.  I learned a lot, happy to share.

replies.author: Karmaroo2020
replies.body:
Here is a prompt to use for generic blender MCP:  

Set up a Blender pipeline on this machine and use it to build a 3D asset, end to end.

**1. Install Blender.** Get a current LTS build, unpack it somewhere stable like `/opt/blender`, and symlink the executable onto the PATH so `blender --version` works from any directory. Confirm the version before continuing.

**2. Wire up the MCP server** so you can drive Blender conversationally: add an MCP server that runs `uvx blender-mcp` over stdio, and install the matching BlenderMCP addon inside Blender itself (the addon opens a socket the server connects to; the server is useless without it). Verify you can query the scene through it before you rely on it.

**3. Understand the split, and respect it.** MCP is for *exploration* — poking at a scene, checking what's there, trying an idea. It is not reproducible and must not be how the asset is produced. **The deliverable is a committed Python script** that builds the model from nothing:

    blender --background --python build_<thing>.py

No `.blend` files as source of truth. A `.blend` is a binary nobody can review, diff, or regenerate. The script *is* the asset.

**4. Build something.** Ask me what to make if it isn't obvious; otherwise pick something with real structure rather than a primitive — a small environment, a vehicle, a prop set. Author it entirely in `bpy`. Export to glTF at the end.

**5. Verify at the byte level, not by vibes.** After every export, run an audit script that parses the exported file and asserts what you claim: vertex/triangle counts within budget, which meshes carry UVs or vertex colors, that vertex colors contain real values rather than defaults, that no object's origin collapsed to (0,0,0) by accident, that expected node names exist. Do this *before* looking at any picture — most defects are cheaper to catch in the bytes.

**6. Then look at it.** Render preview shots from several angles, open the images, and judge them yourself. Fix what's wrong in the script and re-run. Don't hand me the first export.

**Two things that will bite you:**

* **The glTF exporter is not deterministic in ordering**, so don't diff exports byte-for-byte to check a change; diff the audited properties instead.
* **Object names are an interface.** If a consuming engine reads names — prefixes for lights, screens, collision — establish that convention up front and put it in the docs, because a rename becomes a functional change, not cosmetics.

Write a short README covering: how to run the build, what the naming conventions mean, the budget, and every trap you hit. Assume the next person has none of your context.
